Below, it shows how many patients had tumour DNA detected in their blood at all, and whether those patients lived shorter or longer than those without it. With the clonal-haematopoiesis filter on, changes that probably come from ageing blood cells rather than the tumour — in genes such as DNMT3A and TET2, or also found in the patient's white blood cells — are left out first, and the figure says how many were removed and what the numbers were without the filter.

help.text: Looks for the value of a measurement — such as tumour mutational burden — that best splits patients into a group that did better and a group that did worse. It tries every reasonable dividing line (from the lowest tenth of patients to the highest) and draws how strongly each one separates survival; the dot marks the best. Because trying many lines and keeping the best always finds something, the view also reshuffles the measurement among the patients a thousand times to see how good a 'best line' chance alone produces, and reports how surprising the real best line is once that search is accounted for. A line found this way needs checking in other patients before anyone relies on it.

help.text: Splits one group of patients — say, lung cancers — into those whose tumour carries one of the well-known, usually treatable cancer-driving changes (EGFR, KRAS, ALK and the rest of the list) and those whose tumour carries none, and then asks which other genes are changed more often in the second group. Those genes are candidates for what drives the tumours without a known driver. Patients whose test did not cover every gene on the list are kept apart, since we cannot tell whether they have a driver. The bar shows how big each group is; in the chart, genes to the right are more common without a known driver.

help.text: Some people are born with a faulty copy of a cancer gene such as BRCA2 in every cell. help.text: HLA class I molecules (HLA-A, -B and -C) show pieces of a tumour's proteins to the immune system. Everyone inherits two copies of each; a person who inherited two identical copies at a gene (homozygous) shows a narrower range of pieces, and a tumour can also lose one copy (HLA loss of heterozygosity) to hide. This shows how common each is in a cohort, and whether patients homozygous at any of the three genes, or whose tumour lost a copy, lived shorter or longer. In patients treated with immunotherapy, homozygosity has been linked to worse survival; in a cohort not limited to them the comparison describes prognosis, not response to treatment.

help.text: For patients who had two kinds of tumour sample tested — usually the original tumour and a later spread of it elsewhere in the body — shows, gene by gene, how often a change was found in both samples, only in the original, or only in the spread. Changes found only in the spread can point to how the cancer adapted, for example to a treatment. The two kinds can also be samples taken before and after a treatment. Without a list of genes, it checks every gene and shows the ones most often found on one side only.

help.text: Asks, gene by gene, whether a mutation changes how patients do on a particular treatment — not just whether it marks a better or worse outlook in general. For each gene it compares patients with and without the mutation twice: among those who received the treatment (upper marker) and among those who did not (lower marker). A gene whose markers sit far apart — say, much worse with the mutation only among the treated — may predict who benefits from that treatment; the right-hand column tests that difference. Treatment here was not assigned at random, and patients had to live long enough to receive it, so a finding is a lead to test properly, not proof.
help.title: What is this?

help.text: A model that predicts survival from which genes are mutated in each patient, in the style of the OncoCast package. It is trained many times, each time on two thirds of the patients and tested on the other third, so every patient's risk score comes from a model that never saw them. Patients are then split into low, intermediate and high risk, and their survival curves are drawn. The list shows the genes the model relied on most, with a hazard ratio above 1 meaning higher risk. Tick "validate" to train on one half of the patients and grade the model on the other half, which it never saw, or name another group of patients under "validate on" to grade it there — for example patients from a different study — with the same risk-group boundaries.
help.title: What is this?

help.text: Answers “how many months, on average, did patients in each group live within the first τ months?” — the shaded area under each survival curve up to τ. The difference between two groups is the months gained or lost in that window, which reads plainly even when the curves cross or only separate late (as with immunotherapy), where a single hazard ratio can mislead. τ is where every group still has at least ten patients followed, unless it is set. Landmark panels ask the same question again among the patients still alive and followed at 6 or 12 months, restarting the clock there. The groups were not randomised, so a difference is a clue, not proof.
help.title: What is this?

help.text: Starts each patient's clock on the day a treatment began — for example their first immunotherapy — and follows them to an outcome that real-world studies use in place of a trial's: when they moved on to their next treatment (time to next treatment), when they stopped this one (time on treatment), or when their cancer was recorded as growing (real-world progression-free survival). Death counts as the outcome too, and patients still followed without it are counted up to their last visit. Each group's curve shows the share not yet there at each month, with the number still followed below. The groups were not randomised to the treatment, so a gap between curves is a clue, not proof that a gene or a group changes how well the treatment works.
help.title: What is this?
